Put another way, the First Intellect's existence, seen as light or as related to God, gives rise to the light of the second intellect. Seen as mixed with the shadow of possibility or as related to itself, it gives rise to the outermost sphere. In both cases, the cause is existence viewed in two different ways.

An acting cause gives its effect what is active and complete in it. But material things are not pure activity: because of matter, they also contain potential and limits. The matter in the agent makes it a particular kind of cause and limits the range of its effect. The matter in what receives the effect helps it receive, but also keeps it from becoming fully complete. This is likely what the author means when he denies that bodily things can give existence in the way a divine cause does. He does not mean that bodies in nature cannot cause anything at all. We observe causes in nature and use them to find the rules that govern natural events. The philosophers explain the special features of kinds of things by their forms, and their motions by what moves them. The point is that bodies do not create the underlying matter or the substantial forms, as a divine cause does.
That is, active bodily powers cannot be divine causes that give existence, even though they can cause changes in nature. This is even less possible for powers that are merely passive or preparatory.

The expression “makes reception possible” answers an objection. We may grant that a bodily power does not bring the later form into existence, but suppose it produces the matter’s readiness to receive it. Would the same difficulty not return? No: the power makes it appropriate to describe the matter as ready; it does not separately bring that readiness into existence. Keep this distinction in mind.

This refers to the teaching that nonexistence is one of the starting points of things that come into being. Aristotle named three: matter, form, and nonexistence. Here, nonexistence means that matter has shed its earlier form; without that, it could not receive the new form.

The commentator offers another account of nonexistence as a starting point. In the earlier account, it is part of what makes up a thing; here, it is part of what allows existence to begin. In one case, nonexistence accompanies matter; in the other, it stands against existence. The discussion becomes clearer if there is change within substance itself. Another way to explain it is that possibility could not exist without nonexistence: possibility means that existence and nonexistence are both open to the thing. Possibility is one reason a thing needs a cause. More broadly, unless we recognize nonexistence at the levels below God's own complete existence, there can be no levels or degrees among beings. Every level below the highest is incomplete in relation to what is above it, even if it is not made of matter and form, or of a general kind and its distinguishing feature. It is made up of being and a lack when compared with what is above it. Only God is simple reality without qualification.
Here “matter” means matter formed into a body, as the word usually does. Prime matter itself has no spatial position. Position comes two stages after it.

The power's action in these two cases is not the same. When it affects something else, it acts as a natural cause. When its effect is in its own matter, it only serves as a channel through which a higher cause's influence first passes. The author confirms this at the end of the chapter: the power is a condition for the matter to receive an effect, not the cause that gives it existence. This does not mean that natural powers and forces do nothing.

The author now gives three results of this principle. First, a bodily power cannot produce an immaterial being, such as a soul, let alone a power that can only be acted upon. Second, bodily powers cannot produce prime matter, which has no spatial position and is so low in the order of things that it nearly resembles nonexistence. Third, they cannot produce bodily form, because a body needs form in order to exist and act, yet a bodily power has no spatial relation to the form in its own body.

An immaterial being has the same relation to all the things it affects, since it has no spatial position. Things that exist in time are therefore timeless in relation to separate intellects, just as timeless things are eternal in relation to the Eternal.

The soul begins as bodily and tied to a spatial position. Through change within its very being, it becomes spiritual. The author also answers the objection by saying that the body's mixture of qualities is a condition for the soul to come into being.
The author explains this later, in the middle of the Journey on the Soul.

This is a fallacy. The fact that the concept of existence is one and applies in the same way does not mean that all the things it describes have the same nature. That would follow only if existence were part of what they are, as “rational animal” is part of the definition of a human being, so the features of that definition apply to humans. But this self-evident concept of existence does not make up the different levels of existence, as we explained near the start of this book.

He seems not to have considered that things can differ in their whole nature, without that difference being made up of a general kind and a distinguishing feature. The most general kinds and the final distinguishing features are examples.

That conclusion does not follow. On this assumption, the cause's existence would itself be composite, so more than one effect could issue from it. Besides, broader kind and distinguishing feature have one existence, especially in simple things. The mind's distinction between them is like its distinction between existence and essence.

We raised this objection earlier, in the discussion of causation: if essences themselves were caused, there would be a problem with individuals that share the same specific essence. Recall that argument.

If you object that al-Razi says God has an essence, I reply: if this objection is meant as a proof, the problem is clear. If it is meant to force us to accept his own assumptions, we can answer that the cause of something that exists must itself exist. So this essence would need existence in order to have an effect. Yet al-Razi treats existence as one and the same in all things.
More precisely, the second of the two senses leads to the first.
“Before” here means before in time. This is enough to refute the claim, because it would mean that an effect comes after its complete cause.
What is described as possible is not limited to a particular time. The universe means everything other than God, and its possible natures are not confined to a time.
This would also make possibility depend on something else, which is impossible on the view being discussed.

The commentator adds a third argument for possibility being eternal. If possibility were not eternal, its opposite—impossibility—would be eternal, which leads to an impossible result. Once that is rejected, possibility must be eternal. He then argues that eternal possibility allows the possibility of eternal existence: a perfect source can always give, and an unrestricted act of giving needs only that a thing be possible in itself. Theologians reject this conclusion, as the objection that follows will show.

One might say that the condition is the prior nonexistence of each event: every event's nonexistence existed from eternity and ended when the event began. But that creates a circle. The end of Zayd's impossibility depends on the end of his nonexistence; his nonexistence ends only when he exists; his existence depends on his possibility; and that possibility depends on the end of his impossibility.

The author is not speaking about things whose very nature is change, but about enduring kinds—such as humans, horses, and cattle—whose individuals replace one another. A clearer example is a person such as Zayd, who plainly came into being even though his possibility is eternal. The answer is that the argument concerns existence in general, which needs only possibility in itself. Zayd's particular existence also needs matter ready to receive him and a link to the Eternal, such as a part of the heavens' motion.
Nothing comes into being while it is already continuing to exist. Coming into being means existing after nonexistence; continuing to exist means existing after already existing.
This would also make possibility depend on something else, which is impossible on the view being discussed.

You may say that the possibility of possibility belongs to it by itself, just as existence belongs to existence by itself. But that would mean possibility itself is an essence, and so one of the possible things; it would still need another possibility. Every essence has its own possibility. Also, this possibility that comes from something else must belong to essences and make them ready to receive the possibility that comes from beyond them.

Otherwise, one option would prevail for no reason, which is impossible. The author does not discuss the other option—that a thing remains possible but becomes independent of a cause—because its problem is clear.

While it continues to exist, the effect remains equally open to either side and needs something to determine which side occurs. Possibility is the basis of that need. This explanation also answers the charge that the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.

This question is meant to show that an effect no longer needs a cause once it exists, even if it remains possible. The commentator replies that one option being more likely does not make the other impossible. The author also gives another answer.

You may object that the question is about what creates the need, not about the thing that needs a cause. The same applies to the earlier claim that nonexistence cannot explain this need. I reply that the real basis of dependence must be what truly depends. As the author explains, coming into being is not itself something that depends; and possibility, taken as an abstract idea, does not depend either. The real sense of possibility is need and dependence. So this argument shows that coming into being is not the basis of dependence, but it does not show that the abstract idea of possibility—the idea that either side may occur—is that basis. The author rejects this sense of possibility elsewhere, unless it is meant only as a way to recognize dependence, not as what makes the thing depend.
Pure relations cannot be identical with God's essence, since they are relations. Negative attributes cannot be identical with it either, since they refer to absence, not to the reality of existence.
More precisely, this is the view of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, who say that God's knowledge involves forms impressed in the divine essence.

This is the view that the fixed forms of all things, which follow the divine names and attributes, are detailed forms of knowledge within God's essence. Unlike the forms described by the Aristotle’s followers, these fixed forms do not come after their source; they are like the meanings of God's names and attributes.
In this view, being knowledgeable and being able are states caused by a feature in the subject. They cannot be separated from that subject.

The commentator objects that necessity is one kind, whether something is necessary in itself or because of something else. Since necessity makes a thing independent, the necessity of an event at the time it exists would also seem to make it independent of a cause. How, then, can coming into being be what makes it need a cause?

Rather, the cause brings about the event: an event is something that exists after not existing, and its existence comes from the cause. Why would the event stop being an event after its first moment? The effect can be necessary in one respect and possible in another. Its existence is necessary once its cause is present, while its essence, considered on its own, remains possible. After the cause acts, possibility is not true of the effect in every sense; it remains true only when we consider the essence by itself. This explains how an effect can continue to depend on a cause while it exists.
Yes, but priority in nature and order is enough; priority in time is not required.

Not necessarily. Two things may both be eternal, yet one may be stronger and the other weaker. The weaker may depend on the stronger, not the other way around. Consider the sun and its light if both are eternal.

This argument rests on a mistaken assumption. Who says that God acts by intention or by a motive added to His essence? The philosophers say He acts through knowledge and willing; the mystical view says He acts through self-disclosure. Even if “intention” means ordinary purpose, a motive may come from within or from outside, and need not apply only to things coming into being. God's action is related to His own essence.

In the theologians' language, an essential attribute is what makes similar things alike and different things unlike. Blackness makes two black things alike, and humanity makes two humans alike; blackness and sweetness differ because one is black and the other sweet. They also use “attribute” for a feature that exists in something else. The subject gives rise to that feature, yet it exists along with the subject for as long as the subject exists.
In the mind's ordering of events, one could insert “then” or “so” between them.
As explained earlier, one of the two absences reveals the other, while the other is what brings it about.

The difficult problem here is how an event that begins in time can be linked to an eternal cause through something between them. It has been called an almost incurable difficulty. For the theologian who holds that the universe as a whole began in time, the difficulty arises in two ways. First, how can God's act begin later if God has always existed and is a complete cause, from which the effect cannot fail to follow? The Necessary Being is necessary in every respect. Philosophers need not face this problem in the same way. Second, how are the events that occur each day connected with God? Philosophers, the Ashʿarites, and the leading thinkers of the religious community agree that nothing gives existence except God: there is no power or strength except through God, the Most High, the Almighty.

The brief answer to the second difficulty is that every new event depends on an eternal source together with a newly arising condition. God also gives existence to that condition, since He alone gives existence in the fullest sense. There are three main accounts of these conditions, none of which the author sets out explicitly here. On the first, they are successive changes in elemental matter, through which fresh states of readiness arise without end. On the second, they are the successive positions of the heavens and the stages of their circular motion. On the third, they are stages in the flowing nature of the heavens and in the continuous change of their very substance. This third account is the author's.

How, on this account, does a changing nature depend on the eternal and unchanging God? The author points to a nature that preserves time and has two aspects: one continually renewed, the other abiding with God. The two are like a cone of light, its tip with God and its base with matter. The tip depends on the eternal God, while successive stages at the base are linked with events and natural things that begin and end. The flowing of this nature belongs to what it is and does not need a further explanation. On the other philosophers' account, the heavens' motion, considered as being between its starting and ending points, is simple and stable in itself though its relations change; thus it depends on the eternal God. Its successive stages, considered as a continuous course, are linked with the events that come to be.
Change belongs to the way a natural thing exists, not to its nature considered on its own. A thing's reality is its nature together with its existence.
